noticias.titulo: How exactly did Trump get so rich on crypto? We explain
noticias.resumen: President Trump has made billions of dollars in his second term — most of it in cryptocurrencies. Democrats are vowing to probe his businesses as they gear up to take over Congress next year.
noticias.texto:
How exactly did Trump get so rich on crypto? We explain
Trump's crypto profits raise alarms for transparency advocates
For the last year, Will Ragland and a team of researchers at the Center for American Progress — a left-leaning think tank in Washington, D.C. — have dedicated themselves to counting how much money President Trump and his family have made in his second term.
So far, they put the total at nearly $3 billion. More than 2 billion dollars of the earnings come from cryptocurrency ventures.
"You could probably combine all of the past presidents' income made during their time in office," Ragland says. "And it wouldn't come close to what we're seeing here."
This unprecedented profit could soon become a major political problem for the president.
After campaigning heavily on an anti-corruption message that resonated with voters, Democrats are promising to make holding Trump and his administration accountable a critical plank of their oversight agenda when they take over both the Senate and the House next year.
From Sen. Elizabeth Warren from Massachusetts to Rep. Robert Garcia from California, prominent Democrats are vowing to hold oversight hearings and hold President Trump and his administration accountable.
"Americans should be secure in the knowledge that their government is focused on their best interests—not on making the President's family richer," Rep. Garcia warned in a letter after the midterms this month warning Trump, his family and his administration to preserve records.
Here's a guide to how Trump made his crypto wealth.
Trump's meme coin
Shortly before his inauguration in early 2025, Trump and now-First Lady Melania Trump each launched their own meme coins — or cryptocurrencies based on Internet memes, cartoon characters, or even jokes.
Trump made over $600 million from the meme coin called $TRUMP, according to the president's own disclosures.
In an effort to drum up demand for the coin, Trump also held two galas for the top holders of $TRUMP. The president promised the closest access to himself to those who invested the most in the coin.
A third gala is scheduled for Sunday at his golf course in Virginia.
Many of the guests for the first event last year were likely to have been foreign, according to media reports. The second dinner, held this year, attracted considerably less interest, though participants also described a significant presence of people from abroad.
For Ragland and other anti-corruption activists, the dinners raise significant concerns about potential conflicts of interest.
"This is a way for foreign investors, foreign countries in some instances, to try and get as much influence as they can and use that as leverage for deals that they want to make that are helpful to them," Ragland says.
Already, top Democrats including Rep. Jamie Raskin from Maryland have launched investigations — and the galas are likely to become an aspect of their oversight into Trump's crypto ventures next year.
A White House spokesperson warned Democrats against pursuing "sham investigations" when contacted by NPR about the Democrats' oversight plans.
"As the President has said, he's willing to work with anyone to continue delivering victories for hardworking Americans," Lauren Bis said in an emailed statement. "If Democrats choose to pursue sham investigations and radical left policies, they are choosing to work against the American people."
A crypto deal with a U.A.E. firm
But the biggest source of Trump's wealth over his second term comes from a crypto venture called World Liberty Financial, which the president's family helped launch even before Trump won the 2024 presidential election.
Working with Steve Witkoff — whom Trump would later appoint as U.S. envoy for the Middle East — as well as Witkoff's son Zack Witkoff, the Trump family started World Liberty Financial late in 2024.
The venture revolves around a type of cryptocurrency called stablecoin (here's an NPR explainer). Zach Witkoff now serves as the CEO of World Liberty Financial.
Just days before Trump's inauguration, World Liberty received a $500 million investment in exchange for 49% of the company.
The buyer? A firm linked to Sheikh Tahnoon bin Zayed Al Nahyan, a member of the United Arab Emirates royal family who serves as the kingdom's national security adviser. The news was first reported by The Wall Street Journal.
The investment was an extraordinary show of faith in a young company that was striving to get a foothold in the crypto sector.
Months later, the U.A.E. earned a substantial concession: The U.S. eased export restrictions, allowing the shipment of about 500,000 of the most advanced American AI chips to the kingdom. The shipment was critical in the U.A.E's ambition to build big AI data clusters and become an AI power.
Democrats have seized on the timing, although President Trump has denied any quid pro quo. In a recent interview with CBS' 60 Minutes, the president said he does not keep track of how much money he makes from his business ventures.
"I devote almost no time to my net worth. I don't care. I make – I have a lotta money, and far more than I ever thought I'd have. And I guess it's gone up. I don't even know," Trump told 60 Minutes correspondent Ross Douthat.
But Will Ragland and his team have tallied up the earnings linked to World Liberty Financial and its stablecoin business: The total, they say, is over $1.7 billion.
World Liberty Financial declined to comment.
Another major deal for Trump's crypto venture
Another key deal with World Liberty Financial helped boost the profile of the company's cryptocurrency — and the Trump family's profits.
Using $2 billion of World Liberty Financial's stablecoin, a separate firm — also led by Sheikh Tahnoon — bought a small stake in a top crypto exchange called Binance last year.
The deal instantly elevated World Liberty Financial's stablecoin into one of the biggest in the market.
Months later, Changpeng Zhao — the convicted founder of Binance who no longer runs the crypto exchange — was pardoned by President Trump. CZ, as he's widely known, still has the biggest stake in Binance and weighs in publicly, including when the exchange got hacked earlier this month.
Meanwhile, the relationship between Binance and World Liberty deepened. Binance actively promoted World Liberty Financial's stablecoin to its customers, further elevating the market valuation of the cryptocurrency to $5 billion, according to The New York Times.
While the relationship has come under scrutiny, Binance has strongly defended the acceptance of World Liberty's cryptocurrency as having been done on its own merits.
"Any suggestion that Binance did anything to support World Liberty Financial or USD1 to gain political favour or influence a legal outcome is false," a spokesperson told NPR in an email, referring to World Liberty's stablecoin. A representative for CZ declined to comment.
But transparency advocates are suspicious — and so are top Democrats. In a widely quoted social message, Rep. Robert Garcia posted a social media message for the Trump family and his administration: "Lawyer up."

noticias.titulo: The U.K. and EU hold a rare summit to strengthen ties
noticias.resumen: A decade after the people of Britain voted to leave the European Union, top EU officials are meeting with Prime Minister Andy Burnham on Friday, looking to mend more fences.
noticias.texto:
The U.K. and EU hold a rare summit to strengthen ties
BRUSSELS — A decade after the people of Britain voted to leave the European Union, top EU officials are meeting with Prime Minister Andy Burnham on Friday, looking to mend more fences, and just perhaps, to pave the way for them to get back together.
Burnham is scheduled to hold just under an hour of talks in Brussels with European Council President António Costa and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen. Then they'll all meet in a plenary session with U.K. government ministers and European commissioners.
Burnham has described the rare EU-U.K. summit — only the second since Britain became the first country to leave the world's biggest trading bloc — as a step toward undoing a decade of damage caused by the divorce.
"The Brexit we were given has not worked. We have lost more than we gained," he said this week.
Burnham has said all options should be on the table for future relations, including rejoining the now-27-nation bloc. But he's stressed that reversing Brexit is just one possible outcome, and far from imminent. It would need the backing not just of British voters, but the unanimous support of a mistrustful EU. Still, he has broken a long political code of silence on the option of rejoining.
Ahead of the meeting, von der Leyen said she wanted it to be "a summit of ambition and concrete results. More opportunities for young people. Easier agrifood trade. And a stronger cooperation on economic security."
Burnham pitched the package of agreements expected to be signed Friday as a way of "cutting costs, keeping prices down in the supermarkets and creating opportunities for young people."
He said "a closer partnership with Europe is good for working people, good for Britain and good for Europe."
The deals are set to include an agreement for up to 100,000 young adults from Britain to live and work in EU countries for up to three years, and the same number of Europeans to come to the U.K.
There will also be an emissions trading agreement and a deal to remove checks on food and agricultural products that will make things cheaper and easier for British exporters to Europe. Burnham says the deals could add a modest 0.4% to Britain's economy.
To get the deals, the U.K. must accept some EU rules and standards that it has no role in setting. Supporters of Brexit say that undermines Britain's independence.
"I'm afraid that the great Brexit debate has just started again," Reform UK leader Nigel Farage told the BBC. He said "it's perfectly clear that this very, very soon becomes a debate about: do we rejoin or do we stay out?"
The war in Ukraine, and the U.K.'s military strength, are drawing the two back together, and the summit provides the EU with an opportunity to discuss stronger cooperation on security and defense, as well as efforts to restrict irregular migration.
"Our security and prosperity are closely intertwined, making a strong partnership between us essential," Costa said ahead of the meeting. "By deepening our cooperation, we can strengthen our ability to address the challenges of our time, strengthen our resilience and promote stability in Europe and beyond."
Nevertheless, feelings remain raw, and EU officials have been reluctant to encourage talk of the U.K. rejoining. They are weary from the shifting demands of seven British prime ministers over the last decade and want real clarity about the country's intentions.
Ireland's ambassador in London, Sonja Hyland, said that when Britain voted for Brexit, "there was a lack of clarity as to exactly what that meant." If Britain wants to reopen negotiations, she said, it must "make a clear decision as to what it wants."

noticias.titulo: Why the U.S. air traffic control system still relies on an 'antique' network
noticias.resumen: The FAA says the telecom outage that led to Friday's nationwide ground stop began with an upgrade to fiber-optic cables. Industry experts say the work is long overdue.
noticias.texto:
Why the U.S. air traffic control system still relies on an 'antique' network
Rossana D'Antonio was at John F. Kennedy International Airport in New York, just about to board a plane back to Los Angeles, when the Federal Aviation Administration declared a nationwide ground stop.
D'Antonio's flight was canceled last Friday, along with thousands of others. She was lucky, and got a seat on a flight Saturday morning.
"By then, of course, the hotels were all booked. And so I spent the night at JFK," she said with a rueful laugh.
D'Antonio is not just a frequent flier. She also is the president-elect of the American Society of Civil Engineers. So her mind went right to infrastructure.
"The very first thing I thought of was, 'We told you so,'" D'Antonio told NPR. "We are reliant on a system that was considered to be state of the art back in the 1980s. This is common knowledge. We've known about it, and we simply haven't acted swiftly enough."
Last week's nationwide ground stop was an unwelcome reminder that the U.S.' air traffic control system runs on antiquated technology.
"We have a patchwork, archaic federal telephone network," the head of the Federal Aviation Administration, Bryan Bedford, said Thursday at Honeywell Aerospace's American Aviation Leadership Summit in Washington. "Which is why we gotta get off [of] it as fast as humanly possible, while maintaining safety."
The FAA is still unsure exactly what caused the telecommunications meltdown that led to the nationwide ground stop, just the second since 9/11. But the agency says it started with work to install a router at a remote facility in Arkansas -- part of an ongoing effort to replace outdated copper wiring with modern fiber-optic cables.
No one disputes that the old equipment is a problem, or that updates now underway should have happened a long time ago. So why is the world's busiest and most complex airspace still running on network technology from the 1980s?
Former FAA and DOT officials say the answer starts with decades of underfunding.
"At its core, it's a money problem," Michael Huerta, a former FAA administrator during the Obama administration, said in an interview last year. "The FAA has been asked to do more with less."
The agency has tried to invest in new technology. But at the same time, Huerta said, the older systems must stay running to keep planes in the air 365 days a year, 24 hours a day.
The older networks are fragile, and expensive to maintain because they're obsolete, former FAA officials say. And it's challenging to connect them with modern equipment designed to run on fiber-optic networks.
"This should have been taken on earlier," said William Voss, a former FAA executive involved in previous modernization efforts back in the 1990s. "It's effectively been eating all the money up trying to run this antique store in the biggest air traffic system in the world."
The FAA got an influx of money last year when Congress allocated $12.5 billion to upgrade the air traffic control system. But Voss warned the task is complicated and daunting.
"There's not a lot of people that have done that in one big leap," he said.
Voss worries the Trump administration is moving too quickly, without allowing enough time for planning and coordination. And he wonders why the failed network upgrade that crippled the nation's airspace was scheduled during a busy Friday afternoon.
"I can't imagine why you do that unless you are just under tremendous schedule pressure," Voss said.
The timing also seems questionable to Dave Spero. He's the national president of Professional Aviation Safety Specialists, the union that represents technicians at the FAA.
"No, I wouldn't do that on a Friday afternoon," he said. "To be safe, I would probably want to schedule it on a midnight shift."
The Government Accountability Office also raised concerns about the speed of modernization work. In a report published in September, the GAO said the administration has been accelerating the timeline of modernization work already underway -- including the telecommunications network that failed on Friday.
"They are basically buying speed at the risk of cost uncertainty and the potential for disruptions in the national airspace," said Kevin Walsh, the director of the GAO's Information Technology and Cybersecurity team, who was the lead on the report.
The GAO report also noted the first phase of the FAA's modernization effort includes more than 11,000 distinct projects with no integrated master plan.
"While that may work, it increases the risk of outages, especially when dealing with these older systems, which are prone to failure," Walsh said.
But the Trump administration defends its approach.
"Some of you will say I'm moving too fast. Some of you say, I'm moving too slow. Um, maybe I'm Goldilocks and I'm going just right here," said Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy after meeting Republican Senators at the Capitol on Tuesday. "But I'll just tell you, the longer we stay on an old rickety network, the less safe it becomes."
There's another reason, experts say, the Trump administration might want to move quickly.
After decades of air traffic control modernization attempts that took longer and delivered less than promised, the FAA wants to show Congress that it's serious this time, said Eric Soskin, a former inspector general at the Department of Transportation.
"That's a powerful signal to say, hey, we're going to get it done. We are going to carry out this important effort," Soskin said.
The FAA still has a lot of modernization work left to do, with the potential for more disruptions ahead, other former agency leaders warned.
"I don't expect another major US shutdown. The FAA is going to avoid that at all costs," said Michael O'Donnell, a former senior executive at the agency.
"We'll get some disruptions, but I don't think it'll be anything like we saw on Friday night … I'd be really shocked and surprised, and a little worried, if that happened again."

noticias.titulo: Some oil giants will now be labeled ‘sustainable’ under EU finance rules
noticias.resumen: The agreement came the same day the EU agreed to delay methane emission rules for fossil fuel companies.
noticias.texto: BRUSSELS — Some of the world’s biggest oil companies will be able to promote themselves as green investments in the EU under an overhaul of the bloc’s sustainable finance rules. EU member countries and lawmakers struck a deal late Thursday to update the Sustainable Finance Disclosure Regulation that will make it easier for private investment earmarked for green activities to flow into new fossil fuel projects. It was Big Oil’s second big European win of the day, after the EU agreed early Thursday to delay methane emission rules for fossil fuel companies for two years. The sustainable finance agreement substantially loosens a proposal by the European Commission to get more money flowing into companies that are switching from dirtier to cleaner business models. The executive decided to overhaul the SFDR, which aims to prevent greenwashing and help investors make sustainable investment decisions, last November. It proposed introducing three new categories for green funds — ESG basics, Transition and Sustainable — which each have progressively stricter sustainability criteria. EU countries and the European Parliament had disagreed over whether fossil fuel companies should be allowed in the new “transition” category. The Commission proposed a blanket exclusion, but member countries pushed for oil companies with greener ambitions to be included. The Parliament, meanwhile, only wanted oil and gas companies to be allowed if they invest more in green activities than in new oil and gas projects over a three-year period. Under Thursday’s final agreement, seen by POLITICO, the EU has ruled that companies will have to spend one-fifth of their capital expenditure on green activities and this will have to “meaningfully” increase “over time” and be measured annually. The increase in green investment cannot be “merely marginal or nominal,” the rules specified. The 20% capex threshold will be reviewed by the Commission in five years. Companies will also have to produce a Paris-aligned emissions reduction plan for some of their emissions. However, downstream emissions — which represent the biggest share of oil and gas companies’ emissions — will not have to be covered by these plans. The EU’s finance chief, Maria Luís Albuquerque, told POLITICO that the final deal was “close enough” to the Commission’s proposal as she left the meeting. The outcome could see big oil and gas companies like France’s TotalEnergies and Spain’s Repsol qualify for financing under the transition category, based on their 2025 capital expenditure. The French oil giant met with the lead Parliament negotiator, Dutch MEP Gerben-Jan Gerbrandy, three times between the start of 2025 and June 2026, according to Parliament documents . Aleksandra Palinska, executive director at sustainable finance NGO Eurosif, said the criteria agreed by the co-legislators on the transition category “fail to distinguish companies genuinely transforming their business models from those making isolated green investments.” Capitals win EU capitals proposed a more lenient approach than the Commission and Parliament, agreeing in June that Big Oil could be included in the transition category if companies spend one-fifth of their capital expenditure on green activities, as defined under the EU taxonomy on sustainable investments. This is despite several EU countries advocating for a move away from fossil fuels and publishing fossil fuel phase-out plans at COP31 this month. Lawmakers in October voted for big oil and gas companies to only be included in the category if they invest more in green activities than in new fossil fuel projects over a three-year period. Several EU countries — including France and Italy — saw the Parliament’s position as a “red line,” according to a document seen by POLITICO, with the final agreement landing closer to what EU capitals wanted. Despite this, Gerbrandy, who led negotiations in Parliament, said he was happy with the agreement. “I think we achieved a result that is in accordance with the criteria I set — credibility and administrative burdens — so I’m very satisfied,” he said.

noticias.titulo: ‘Staff deserve answers’ on Commission cyberattack, union says
noticias.resumen: EU executive “yet to send a single update to all staff" about recent cyberattack, union email says.
noticias.texto: BRUSSELS — A European Commission staff union has hit out at the EU executive for keeping officials in the dark after they first heard about a major cyberattack against the EU institution when it was reported by POLITICO. A cyberattack against the Commission potentially compromised swaths of personal data at the EU executive and left staff unable to input salary and leave information, POLITICO first reported on Thursday. The Commission has since publicly acknowledged the incident but it is “yet to send a single update to all staff, let alone provide a comprehensive explanation of the incident,” Cristiano Sebastiani, chair of the European Commission branch of the Renouveau & Démocratie (R&D) union, wrote in an email seen by POLITICO. The lack of internal communication is “unacceptable,” he wrote in the email, titled “Staff deserve answers now.” “It’s simply inconceivable that news outlets around the world are covering the incident while staff are still waiting for their first direct update from the Commission,” he wrote, adding that current and retired colleagues have written to R&D with concerns. The union has several thousand members, Sebastiani said in a comment. Some staff told R&D that managers denied a cyberattack had taken place and said the incident was a routine technical issue, Sebastiani wrote in the email. The lack of communication is especially grave because internal HR systems are affected, meaning sensitive personal data may be at risk, the union representative wrote. He called for the Commission to immediately explain the incident to all staff, including information about what data was affected, and to carry out an independent review. The Commission has informed the European Data Protection Supervisor, the internal EU data watchdog, a spokesperson for the regulator said. The Commission did not immediately respond to a request about the union email. Spokesperson Thomas Regnier said on Thursday that the Commission took “the necessary steps in response to a detected cyber campaign,” adding that individual systems were targeted and that “in line with our standard practice, we have informed those concerned.”

noticias.titulo: Brussels to link UK-EU summit package to tuition fee demands
noticias.resumen: Brussels denies it is taking Britain "hostage" despite insisting student fees are part of wider "package."
noticias.texto: BRUSSELS — Andy Burnham’s EU summit agreements will hinge on a further deal to cut tuition fees for European students studying in Britain, EU capitals have insisted. Negotiators on Thursday night put the finishing touches to deals on agrifood, emissions trading and youth visas — along with a slate of other commitments to closer cooperation under negotiation for the past 18 months. But the EU signaled on Friday morning that its adoption of the agreements hinges on London agreeing to cut tuition fees for EU students to lower home rates, according to a statement set to be approved by ambassadors. “The Council agrees that adoption of the Council Decisions on signing of the ETS, SPS and YES agreements will not precede the conclusion of the negotiations on the supplementing Agreement providing for equal treatment on tuition fees,” a draft of the statement seen by POLITICO says. The statement is expected to be formally adopted on Friday morning by written procedure, an EU diplomat said. A second EU diplomat said: “You can see this as a clear signal from Brussels that this is a package deal.” But they added that there was a “political commitment” to get fees over the line: “We just need to work out the details — and that’s not happening today.” While there is no binding clause in today’s summit agreement linking the trade and youth experience deals with the tuition fee cut, the separate statement drawn up by the EU council effectively says the EU could block their implementation through its own processes if talks on fees do not conclude. Asked about the link between the four deals, an EU official said: “What we have agreed is that we will complete this in six months. I think this is an important element. So let’s hope that everything can go ahead.” However, the official insisted: “We don’t take anyone hostage here.” This is a developing story. Click here for updates.

noticias.titulo: Germany says investors ready to spend €25B to buy TikTok Europe
noticias.resumen: Germany and Austria floated the initiative earlier this week, citing concerns about the Chinese-owned company's influence on European democracy.
noticias.texto: BRUSSELS — The German government has found investors interested in investing as much as €25 billion to buy the majority of TikTok’s EU operations, Berlin’s culture minister Wolfram Weimer told reporters on Friday. “We have spoken to a lot of investors already,” he said. “It’s a pan-European initiative and we think that they are able to invest around about 25 billion euros in that kind of business. And TikTok Europe should be open to sell 75% to 80% of the shares.” Germany and Austria floated the Trump-style initiative earlier this week, citing concerns about TikTok’s influence on European democracy. A TikTok spokesperson Friday dismissed the push as “nonsense,” saying the company is “already subject to comprehensive European law, including the Digital Services Act and the GDPR, which provide clear legal frameworks for any company investing and operating in Europe.” U.S. President Donald Trump forced the sale of the American arm of TikTok to U.S. investors earlier this year by threatening to ban the app domestically citing national security concerns. The move was criticized as a way to keep a political grip on the country, as well as the fact that the investors were close Trump allies like Oracle founder Larry Ellison. “The scheme is the same as the Americans did under the leadership of Oracle” said Weimer, who added that investors in five European countries were interested without specifying which ones. The culture minister spoke to reporters before a meeting with his peers where he would try to gather more support, he said. POLITICO parent company, Germany’s Axel Springer, has reportedly been interested in being part of a deal, and a spokesperson said they would be open to it. The Berlin-based media conglomerate wasn’t immediately available to respond to POLITICO’s request for comment on Weimer’s remarks. This article has been updated.

noticias.titulo: Emmanuel Macron hosts Kamala Harris at Elysée
noticias.resumen: The French leader is hosting the former vice president in a "private capacity," the Elysée said.
noticias.texto: PARIS — French President Emmanuel Macron will host former U.S. Vice President Kamala Harris at the Elysée Palace on Friday, according to his office. Macron is meeting Harris in “a private capacity for a brief courtesy meeting in the presence of her husband, as he sometimes does at the request of certain former leaders,” the Elysée said in a statement. French news outlets La Lettre and Intelligence Online initially reported that Macron and Harris were going to have dinner together, which the Elysée office later confirmed, according to one of the journalists who obtained the information. However, Macron’s office later said the two would only have a private meeting. The face-to-face comes shortly after the Democrats’ emphatic victory in U.S. midterm elections and as strains grow between Paris and Washington over peace talks on the war in Ukraine. Macron and U.S. President Donald Trump, who defeated Harris in the 2024 presidential election, have had a hot-and-cold relationship in recent years. The two recently traded barbs over the rioting in France last month, which Trump and his allies attributed to unchecked immigration — comments the French leader called “stupid.” Macron’s relationship with Harris has been smoother . Harris is reportedly keeping the door open to running for president again in 2028 , by which time Macron will no longer be in office. The French president will leave office in May next year, as he is constitutionally barred from serving a third consecutive term. POLITICO has reached out to a Harris representative for comment. Marcelo Wesfried contributed to this report. This story has been updated.

noticias.titulo: Russia hits 3 Kyiv bridges in major attack, while Poland reports airspace violation
noticias.resumen: The overnight strikes, which killed at least five people across Ukraine, came hours after Vladimir Putin vowed a painful response to Ukraine’s attacks on the Crimean bridge.
noticias.texto: Russia launched a massive missile and drone attack on Ukraine overnight, killing at least five people and damaging three of Kyiv’s main bridges across the Dnipro River — while Poland reported a violation of its airspace. The strikes came hours after U.S. President Donald Trump called into a meeting of Ukraine’s European allies from Air Force One and said Russian President Vladimir Putin was serious about peace negotiations. In Kyiv, three people were killed and about 15 were injured, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said . Ballistic missiles damaged the Podilsko-Voskresenskyi crossing and the Darnytskyi bridge and hit the Southern Bridge again, prompting Klitschko to urge residents not to drive into the city and employers to let staff work from home. “The enemy’s missile attack on Kyiv is ongoing,” he added. In Lviv, a major city near the Polish border, seven people were injured when a strike hit the ticket offices at a railway station, Governor Maksym Kozytskyi said . Air defenses were “in continuous action for nearly 6 hours,” he said , and an attack on an energy facility forced emergency power cuts across the region. In Poland, authorities alerted residents of the Lublin and Subcarpathian regions to an air threat early Friday, and Rzeszów airport suspended flights. Prime Minister Donald Tusk said he had been briefed on “the violation of Polish airspace” near the Ukrainian border and added that, “There is currently no threat from the air. The relevant services are on site.” The strikes came hours after Putin vowed a response “much more painful” than Ukraine’s attacks on the Crimean bridge — and after the Kremlin boss said Europeans should come to Moscow to discuss joining peace talks. Russia began targeting Kyiv’s bridges in early October. Veronika Melkozerova contributed to this report.

Rasmus Buchsteiner analysiert, warum sie zögert, wie sich Hubertus Heil in Stellung bringt und was das für Lars Klingbeil bedeutet. Auf den Straßen formiert sich weiter Protest von Jugendlichen: Die Initiative „Gen Z regelt“ demonstriert gegen die Wehrpflicht und für mehr Bildungsinvestitionen. Nach Ausschreitungen an Halloween erklärt Luis Bobga, Sprecher der Grünen Jugend, im 200-Sekunden-Interview, wie sich seine Organisation von Chaoten abgrenzt, wie der Frust wächst und warum er vor der Rhetorik von Innenminister Alexander Dobrindt warnt. Auf das Dreiertreffen in Shenzhen zwischen Donald Trump, Wladimir Putin und Xi Jinping reagiert Europa in Berlin mit einem trotzigen „jetzt erst recht!“. Dabei gibt es überraschende Signale von Donald Trump in Richtung der „Koalition der Willigen“. Hans von der Burchard berichtet davon und ordnet ein, was Sicherheitsgarantien für die Ukraine wirklich bedeuten würden. Das Berlin Playbook als Podcast gibt es jeden Morgen ab 5 Uhr. noticias.titulo: Delay Another Day: How James Bond can save the EU
noticias.resumen: A series of EU-themed 007 movies? Yes please.
noticias.texto: Welcome to Declassified, a weekly humor column . First the bad news: This POLITICO editor did not make it to the final round of auditions to become the next James Bond, on the spurious grounds of “not meeting any of the criteria.” So begrudging congratulations to Robert Pattinson . Now the good news: I have been asked to write a series of James Bond films based on European Union policies. These will be shown in movie theaters around the globe as a way to expand knowledge of what the EU actually does beyond the square kilometer around the Berlaymont. Pattinson will star as Bond, although as the EU is funding the project, we have been forced to cast Ursula von der Leyen as his boss, M. Budgetary constraints mean that instead of swanky cocktail bars and high-rolling casinos, late-night scenes will be filmed inside the Hairy Canary pub and at Maison Antoine friterie . There are nine films planned. Here are the synopses: Dr. Non — In which Bond tries to scrap the need for unanimity in the Council and replace it with permanent use of qualified majority voting. Omnibussy — Bond tries to make life easier for Europeans by slashing red tape but runs into opposition from frustrated industry groups and concerned NGOs. The Man With The Golden Envelope — A faithful, true-to-life recreation of Qatargate. A View To A Kill Switch — Our hero is tasked with fitting an emergency mechanism into an artificial intelligence system when it starts to behave dangerously. Alas, he is thwarted because Europe is not a global player in AI. To avoid this being a rather disappointing end to the film, it will be swiftly followed by… Quantum Computing of Solace — Which sees 007 appointed as a seconded national expert to help drive progress on the EU Quantum Act. Never Say Never Again — In which Bond accompanies Prime Minister Andy Burnham on a trip to Brussels to discuss closer U.K.–EU relations in an (ultimately futile) attempt to reverse Brexit. Guest starring Nigel Farage as supervillain Nigel Farage. The World Is Not Enough (the film’s producers reserve the right to change the title to Diamonds Are Forever ) — Despite a cost-of-living crisis, the Friends of Cohesion group of free-spending EU countries tries to preserve as much funding as possible for the EU’s poorer regions in the next long-term budget. Bond joins the group as they offer unlimited martinis. License To Chill — The British spy travels around Europe trying to find out what EU lawmakers actually do during a green week, and on Fridays, and on Thursday afternoons. For Your Eyes Only — In which Bond tries to improve transparency within the legislative process by eavesdropping on a trilogue. CAPTION COMPETITION “Another tense moment in the final of the EU Charades Championship. ” Can you do better? Email us at pdallison@politico.eu or get in touch on X @POLITICOEurope . Last time, we gave you this photo: Thanks for all the entries. Here’s the best one from our mailbag — there’s no prize except the gift of laughter, which I think we can all agree is far preferable to cash or booze. “So many species we thought were dead are re-emerging throughout the German countryside: Blue Cornflower, Meadowsweet, Neo-Fascism … ” by Tom Morgan

noticias.titulo: UK ‘playing catch up’ with Nordic countries on crisis preparations, says minister
noticias.resumen: Dan Jarvis told POLITICO’s Westminster Insider that Britain has “a lot we can learn” from Norway, which advises citizens to keep enough food and water to survive for a week.
noticias.texto: LONDON — The U.K. is “playing catch-up” with Nordic allies in its plans to deal with disruption from threats such as natural disasters or cyberattacks that would halt critical infrastructure, Britain’s security minister has said. Dan Jarvis said there is a “lot that we can learn” from Scandinavian countries about preparing citizens for a scenario where basic services are interrupted. Jarvis told POLITICO’s Westminster Insider podcast that “lots of things keep me awake at night,” when asked about threats including hostile states attempting to sabotage undersea cables and cyberattacks that shut down supermarket freezers across Europe. He added: “I’ve just recently returned from Norway, where I was talking with Scandinavian partners about the work that they do to ensure that they are as resilient as possible. “And I think there’s quite a lot that we can learn from them and from other partners in Europe. In truth, there is a bit of catch-up that we’re playing here in the United Kingdom.” The U.K. government launched a campaign called “be ready” in October, advising people to stock up on supplies to sustain themselves for three days, including bottled water, non-perishable food, cash, a torch and an FM radio. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said last month that Britain had been playing catch-up “too often in the past.” By contrast, Norway launched an “emergency preparedness” campaign for its citizens in 2018. In 2024, it updated the advice to stockpile supplies for seven days, up from three. The U.K. government is not currently considering extending its recommended time period beyond three days. However, Jarvis rejected an accusation by peers in the House of Lords that the government is not being transparent enough with the public about the risks. The National Resilience Committee said this week that despite the “be ready” campaign, “the Government appears complacent and the UK is underprepared.” Jarvis pointed out a national risk register that highlights widespread power outages, the loss of drinking water and terrorist and state threats as among the most significant risks to the U.K. He added: “If you look at the things that I’ve said in Parliament on the record [and] the conversations that we’re having nationally about the nature of the world that we are living in, I think there is a lot of conversation about the different threats that we face.” He added: “There is a bit of balance to be struck because we absolutely don’t want to alarm the public — but we do want the public to be alert, we want the public to be prepared.” Jarvis downplayed concerns that some in the U.K. government felt after Cabinet ministers joked about their personal stockpiles — including Housing Secretary Angela Rayner, who said hers would include “mascara, concealer, a bottle of Sauvignon Blanc, some baked beans and a tin of custard.” “As the security minister, there are lots of things that I worry about at any one time. That isn’t one of them,” he said. “I think it’s quite helpful in terms of promoting the conversation. I think it’s quite helpful in terms of focusing people’s minds about what they would do in their own households. “That’s the essence of this campaign. It’s about making sure that there is that resilience in households … so I’m entirely relaxed that people are having a conversation about Sauvignon Blanc or whatever it might be.” Jarvis said he had “obviously followed my own guidance” when building his own home stockpile, including a radio and torch, and had not added any special treats beyond the checklist. He does, however, have a ready supply of eggs at home. “I’ve always found it incredibly relaxing to keep chickens, not least when you have a reasonably busy and demanding job,” he said. “There’s something very peaceful about them.” Find the full episode of Westminster Insider “Stockpiling Britain: Does Westminster know something we don’t?” here .

noticias.titulo: 5 takeaways from the Spanish election debate
noticias.resumen: The two main party leaders clashed over corruption, migration and the economy, as polls point to a possible conservative government backed by the far right.
noticias.texto: MADRID — Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez and center-right People’s Party leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo traded blows in a combative televised debate on Thursday night, making a final pitch to voters ahead of a general election that could usher in a right-wing government backed by the far-right Vox party. The personal animosity between Sánchez and Feijóo was evident during the showdown as the two leaders clashed over migration, corruption, the economy and public services. Feijóo portrayed Sánchez’s government as incompetent and ethically compromised, and Sánchez accused the conservative of being out of step with Europe by embracing Vox. Looking beyond the continent, Sánchez cast himself as a progressive counterweight to Donald Trump and the global far right, while Feijóo urged him to focus less on international affairs and more on the problems facing Spaniards at home. The latest POLITICO poll puts Feijóo’s PP at 29.5%, narrowly ahead of Sánchez’s Socialists on 27.2%, with just 10 days to go before Spaniards head to the ballot box. While the two parties are effectively neck and neck, the prime minister faces an uphill battle to remain in power. Vox is polling at 19.6%, putting the right-wing bloc close to half the vote — and Feijóo in a strong position to form the next government. Meanwhile, the two main parties to the left of the Socialists, Frente Amplio and Podemos, are polling at a combined 8.1%, leaving Sánchez’s camp with little room to build a governing majority. With that polling picture, both Sánchez and Feijóo approached Thursday’s debate as an opportunity to sway undecided voters and the 55% of the electorate who are not yet certain they will cast a ballot . POLITICO breaks down the showdown … Sánchez and Feijóo shake hands for the cameras before a debate where the personal animosity was evident. | Oscar Del Pozo/AFP via Getty Images A record under fire Feijóo sought to present himself as a steady hand while portraying Sánchez’s record in office as one of mismanagement, invoking this year’s two deadly train disasters as evidence. The PP leader tied the deterioration of Spain’s high-speed rail network , which was once a source of national pride, to government corruption and neglect, asking Sánchez whether he really believed passengers could still travel by train without fear. “I myself have taken high-speed trains 130 times over the past few years,” he said. “And I thank God that I am nonetheless able to attend this debate tonight.” Feijóo also seized on Spain’s deepening housing crisis, which Sánchez cited as the main reason for calling the snap election , to question what the government had achieved since taking office in 2018. The prime minister struggled to rebut Feijóo’s charge that he had failed to deliver promised homes, repeating his vow to enact progressive housing measures if reelected. Feijóo also sought to undermine Sánchez’s record by attacking his government’s integrity, rattling off a list of scandals and judicial investigations involving people in the prime minister’s inner circle. Sánchez countered by accusing the PP of being “the most corrupt party in the history of this country” and citing a string of court cases in which party figures were found to have benefited from kickbacks and illegal payments. Feijóo dismissed those scandals as ancient history and sought to cast himself as the “decent” leader Spain deserves. “Without you, there would be no corruption in this country,” Feijóo told the prime minister, vowing to “clean up” Spain if elected. ‘You can’t eat the GDP’ The two leaders offered sharply contrasting diagnoses of Spain’s economy — and competing promises on how to fix it. Sánchez reeled off figures to tout Spain’s strong growth and job creation under his watch, while Feijóo challenged whether those gains were making a difference in ordinary Spaniards’ lives. Accusing the prime minister of having “crushed the middle class,” he sharply said that voters “can’t eat the GDP.” In a bid to remedy the cost of living crisis, Feijóo proposed far-reaching tax cuts. Sánchez warned against this approach and a “180-degree turn” in Spain’s economic policy, pointing out that six in 10 households receive more from the welfare state than they pay. He further pledged to pass a law mandating an annual minimum wage increase until it amounts to 60% of the average wage. Sánchez tried to corner Feijóo by asking whether he would keep pensions indexed to inflation — a sensitive issue in a country where people aged 65 and over account for 28% of the electorate. Although a PP official recently cast doubt on the system, saying it could soon “collapse,” the conservative leader said he would not alter it. Feijóo also attacked Sánchez for failing to pass a national budget since 2023, promising his government would present and secure approval for a budget every year. Who’s out of step with Europe? The emergence of migration as one of the key issues of the campaign is something new in Spanish elections and is strongly tied to the rise of Vox. The arrival of more than 70,000 undocumented migrants in Spain’s North African exclave of Ceuta in July helped push the issue higher up voters’ list of concerns. Sánchez defended the role of migration in Spain’s growth model, arguing it was key to ensuring the country’s future as its native-born population ages. But Feijóo linked the issue to “insecurity,” promising tighter controls. That prompted the prime minister to accuse the conservative leader of “stigmatizing” migrants, who he said represent “a great opportunity” for Spain. The EU has tightened its migration policies in recent years, with five member countries backing plans for deportation hubs in Rwanda just this week. Feijóo accused Sánchez of pursuing a liberal approach that puts Spain at odds with the rest of the bloc. “You’re a problem for Europe on migration policy. Not my words: 22 European prime ministers have said that,” Feijóo said, referring to a letter from EU leaders criticizing the government’s handling of the Ceuta crisis. Migrants arrive on Tarajal beach after crossing the border between Spain and Morocco in Ceuta on July 31, 2026. | Adri Salido/Getty Images Sánchez turned the accusation around, arguing that Feijóo was the one out of step with Europe’s mainstream because of his willingness to govern with Vox. He pointed to German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, whose party refuses to cooperate with the far-right Alternative for Germany, and challenged the PP to explain why it was prepared to do the opposite. ‘Less Trump, more trains’ Sánchez sought to use the portions of the debate focused on foreign policy to return to safe terrain, casting himself as an internationally respected progressive leader standing up to Trump and the global far right — a contrast likely to resonate with Spaniards, 87% of whom have an unfavorable view of the U.S. president. He argued his opposition to the wars in Gaza and Iran had helped Spain consolidate itself as a “beacon” in a world darkened by the rising far right and “techno-oligarchs” seeking to undercut democratic values and social progress. But Feijóo ridiculed Sánchez for focusing more on global affairs than on Spaniards’ day-to-day concerns and called for “less Trump and more trains.” Citing the Ceuta migration crisis, he accused the prime minister of undermining Spain’s global standing and failing to protect the country’s territorial integrity, questioning the government’s ambiguous position on Morocco’s role in this summer’s surge. The two also clashed over defense spending, with Sánchez defending his decision to refuse to bow to Trump’s demands to increase expenditures and questioning how Feijóo intends to finance the higher spending targets. In an exclusive interview with POLITICO, the PP leader declined to commit to NATO’s goal of spending 5% of GDP on defense. No love lost, no punches pulled The poor relationship between the two leaders has been obvious to Spaniards for years, but it was on full display on Thursday night. They arrived at the debate set 20 minutes early and spent that time in silence, reading their notes, without exchanging a word or even looking at each other. Feijóo and Sánchez adopted sharply contrasting strategies: while the conservative leader went on the offensive from the opening bell, Sánchez tried to project composure. Feijóo was relentless in his attacks on the prime minister, whose decency he questioned at several points in the debate. Calling out Sánchez for failing to attend the funeral for the victims of the recent train disaster in Urda, the conservative leader reminded his opponent that he had been “dancing at a rally” a mere 48 hours after the tragedy. “If a family member of yours had died, would you have started dancing, too?” Following the debate, a Socialist official said it had been an exhibition of “good politics versus bad manners” and said Sánchez hadn’t “gone after the committed voters, but rather the more moderate wing.” Polling shows undecided voters are disproportionately women and centrists or center-left voters.

noticias.titulo: ‘He who pays the piper calls the tune’: Czech media-freedom attack is part of wider EU malaise, ex-commissioner Věra Jourová says
noticias.resumen: Věra Jourová, former values commissioner and vice-president of the EU Commission, warns of the consequences of abolishing licence fees in the Czech Republic, whilw warning of numerous attacks on media freedom across Europe.
noticias.texto:
November has come around again, and at least in Czech Republic, it comes in a particularly turbulent year.
Those who can think as far back as 1989 may recall the wonderful and hopeful atmosphere of the Velvet Revolution. And if you smell a euphoric nostalgia in that sentence, your nose is working well.
I vividly remember people in the streets, united by the common enemy of Bolsheviks and the Communist party’s idiotic administration. Czechs revolted against a regime kept alive by most of its people surviving with bent backs.
And this year’s protests in my country took place under the slogan: “Don’t touch our fees”.
But most of us know that thinking of the controversial media bill merely as a “fees” issue is diversionary and dangerous.
Of course, it is possible to fund public service media from the state budget; many EU member states do just that.
But in the Czech context, the step is clearly an effort by politicians in government to take control of public TV and radio.
Some lawmakers do not even bother to hide their mentality of “He who pays the piper calls the tune.”

noticias.titulo: Listen: Europe relaxes methane rules while pledging to cut emissions at COP31
noticias.resumen: Negotiators from the European Parliament and the 27 EU member states agreed yesterday to postpone some of the rules aimed at cutting methane emissions. This happened while COP31 was still underway, with the EU pledging to reduce emissions globally. Can the EU be trusted to tackle greenhouse gas emissions?
noticias.texto: Production: By Europod , in co-production with Sphera Network . EUobserver is proud to have an editorial partnership with Europod to co-publish the podcast series “Briefed” hosted by Léa Marchal. The podcast is available on all major platforms . Find the full transcript below : Negotiators from the European Parliament and the 27 EU member states agreed yesterday to postpone some of the rules aimed at cutting methane emissions. This happened while COP31 was still underway, with the EU pledging to reduce emissions globally. Can the EU be trusted to tackle greenhouse gas emissions? In 2024, the EU adopted its methane regulation. So, what does it actually say? It requires companies in the energy sector to monitor and measure methane emissions from their operations, for example, during gas production. It also restricts venting and flaring. These are two ways of releasing excess gas into the atmosphere: either by releasing it directly or by burning it. Both contribute to global warming. Companies are also required to detect and repair methane leaks from their infrastructure. The regulation was also supposed to impose new requirements on imports of gas, coal and oil starting next year. But that will no longer be the case. In record time, the EU’s co-legislators have agreed to postpone some of these requirements by two years. Read more EU gives oil and gas importers until 2029 on methane checks, rules out more delay Importers will not have to demonstrate that methane emissions from the production of the gas, oil and coal they buy are properly monitored and verified until 2029. As a reminder, methane is responsible for roughly one third of global warming. In the end, the requirement to comply with maximum methane-intensity limits will only come into force in 2031. Why did the EU agree to this legislative rollback? The EU argues that the postponement is necessary in the context of the crisis in the Middle East. This, even though the commission has repeatedly said that there is no risk to gas supplies for the coming winter. Earlier this year, the US ambassador to the EU, Andrew Puzder, criticised the methane regulation, arguing that it would severely discourage exporters from selling to the EU, including American companies. More than twenty organisations representing the fossil fuel industry in Europe and the US also called on the commission to postpone the implementation of the rules applying to fossil fuel imports. Read more ‘Made in Europe’ and low-carbon rules up for debate as EU eyes industrial law deal Two organisations representing the oil and gas industry commissioned a study from Wood Mackenzie, with the following findings: If the methane regulation were implemented as planned, up to 43 percent of EU gas imports could be jeopardised after 2027. This helped convince a majority of EU countries to call for a postponement. Environmental NGOs, however, dispute the industry’s figures. They commissioned a study of their own, which found no risk to gas supplies after 2027. This is the result of an intense lobbying campaign by fossil fuel companies and the Trump administration, said Jutta Paulus, German MEP from the Greens group. Following the agreement, her fellow MEP Dimitris Tsiodras, a Greek from the EPP, defended the decision, saying it provided realistic deadlines and the legal certainty that energy suppliers and operators needed, while maintaining ambition on methane emissions. But here’s the thing: in the end, the actual means to cut methane emissions in imports are just nonexistent: The new limits on methane intensity will not come into force until 2031.

noticias.titulo: [Interview] Scottish priority is to rejoin the EU after Brexit ‘badly damaged’ UK, Scotland’s Europe minister says
noticias.resumen: Scotland, which wants to rejoin the EU and leave the United Kingdom, has pushed for more free movement and less red tape for food and drink exports ahead of a UK-EU summit. Brexit left the UK "badly damaged", Stephen Gethins said.
noticias.texto: Scotland, which wants to rejoin the EU and leave the United Kingdom, has pushed for more free movement and less red tape for food and drink exports ahead of a meeting between the leaders of Britain and EU. Brexit has left the UK “badly damaged”, Scotland’s Europe minister Stephen Gethin said in an interview with EUobserver. He discussed Scottish interests, as Britain and the EU seek tighter relations. What are Scotland’s priorities at the EU-UK summit in Brussels? Stephen Gethins : I think it’s very important to be straightforward and tell you the context in which we’re having this conversation. Scotland voted to remain in the EU twice [In 1975, the UK voted to remain in the European Community and in 2016 most Scottish voters cast their ballots against Brexit]. Opinion polls tell us that three‑quarters of the population would vote to rejoin. Bluntly, our priority is to rejoin the EU. And we feel that anything that brings us closer in line with the rest of Europe helps. Leaving the EU is costing Scotland £9m (€10.7m) per day in terms of lost tax revenues. And that’s before you’ve even considered business being harder and fewer rights for UK citizens, who now have less rights than citizens in any other Western European democratic country. Read more UK-EU summit to see mutual love-bombing, but British must decide what to do next Leaving the EU was catastrophic, which is why I refused to vote to trigger Article 50 , and I stand by that decision. We obviously want to see alignment on food and drink, since it has become harder to import into the EU. We want to see further opportunities for young people, ideally a return to freedom of movement – anything that helps to unpick the damage of being outside the EU. But we have to be mindful of unintended consequences, and we must respect devolution , because we don’t obviously have the treaties in place that the European states do when they interact with each other. We lost the helpful umbrella of the EU that respects decentralisation, unlike the UK. Read more ‘Emperor’s New Clothes’: Burnham breaks 10-year taboo on Brexit The Scottish National Party has campaigned to break away from the United Kingdom, with EU membership lauded as a potential benefit. But under prime minister Andy Burnham, Britain is cosying up to the union anyway. So would you prefer EU accession via a newly independent Scotland or as part of the UK?
